name: Ray & Porcell
label: Revelation
lede: Ray Cappo and John Porcelly made two songs with a drum machine that cost about $10, and Revelation pressed 5,000 copies. The window photo on the sleeve has outlasted both songs.

eras.title: A sampler, a four-track and no drummer
eras.text: Youth of Today had just finished its first run. Ray Cappo had joined a temple and was sleeping at Porcell's apartment, where Porcell had a sampler and a drum machine and wanted to write something that sounded nothing like Youth of Today.

years.h: Porcell's demo is named for its spot on a 4-track tape
years.p: Porcell records a rough electronic demo on a sampler, sequencer and drum machine and calls it Track 4. Dylan Schreifels, Walter Schreifels's younger brother, helps him arrange it.
years.xp:
Porcell said the NYHC scene was changing around him, and that [[Quicksand|3c9f8bef-a658-4204-9ee8-7e95d2535b32]] coming up made him want to experiment. His touchstones were [[Dag Nasty|4709dd69-1034-4634-9e88-d1099453b192]], [[Embrace|9d1ad8e3-8740-429a-bdc5-52f96a9c4431]], '80s Iggy Pop and the Sisters of Mercy.

His own reason, he told No Echo: "We wanted to use a drum machine because we wanted to do something a little different."

years.h: Ray Cappo writes Fame and Broken Glass before flying to India
years.p: Staying at Porcell's place, Cappo writes the words and melodies for Porcell's two songs Fame and Broken Glass, quickly and on the spot.

years.cap: Two figures on park steps, inner spread of the 7" sleeve
years.h: A $10 drum machine and an afternoon at [[Don Fury|0bec484f-b890-4823-af64-0e48530f6f6f]]'s
years.p: Nobody plays drums: the beat comes from a machine Porcell bought for about $10 in Manhattan's Music District. Cappo sings and Porcell plays everything else.
years.xp:
Revelation's Jordan Cooper says the whole 7" grew out of Porcell's little electronic demo, and that he had to keep pushing a reluctant Porcell to release it.

Porcell didn't want to call it Ray and Porcell either. Cooper: "Eventually, I think I just kept suggesting to just call it 'Ray and Porcell'." It stuck.

eras.title: Two faces in a window
eras.text: Revelation pressed 5,000 copies of a two-song record with no drummer and no hardcore tempo. Kids loved it or hated it, and the cover photo became bigger than either song.

years.h: Revelation REV 23 puts Ray & Porcell on a 7"
years.p: Two songs, Fame and Broken Glass. The first pressing is 4,000 on black vinyl and 1,000 on purple.
years.xp: A second, final pressing of just 100 on black came in photocopied, hand-numbered sleeves. RevHQ has since reissued it on opaque blue, 550 copies.

years.cap: Back sleeve of the 7", with the Don Fury recording credit and Legenzowski's photo credit, 1991
years.h: Two men at a window in a downtown office building
years.p: Photographer Raymond Legenzowski, who'd shot for Nike, catches Cappo and Porcell looking out over Manhattan. Most of his other frames from that day are lost.
years.xp:
Porcell's version: "Ray and I were looking out of the window because we couldn't believe how incredible the view was."

The picture outlived the record. The clothing brand Wear Dinner built merch around it, and co-owner Damien Moyal says they declared an International Ray & Porcell 7" Day.

years.big: People either loved it or really hated it.
q: I've never been terribly concerned with other people's opinion of me.
years.h: Hardcore kids can't agree on a drum machine
years.p: Porcell on how fans of Youth of Today took the new songs, which had no drummer and no hardcore tempo.

years.h: Cappo goes Krishna-conscious with [[Shelter|d5157104-76b1-4b8b-90c2-9ff994f940db]], Porcell follows after [[Judge|3827fbb6-e219-4e2d-9af8-35cc9a7d8d8e]]
years.p: Cappo puts his Krishna-conscious hardcore into [[Shelter|d5157104-76b1-4b8b-90c2-9ff994f940db]], and Porcell plays with him there once [[Judge|3827fbb6-e219-4e2d-9af8-35cc9a7d8d8e]], his band with [[Mike Ferraro|edffc714-f0a2-4d6c-b4c0-dc31e713481c]], ends in 1991.
